title: Denoising Is Stein: Moment Accessand a Resource Hierarchy for LearningHidden Structure in Diffusion Models

paper.title: Denoising Is Stein: Moment Access and a Resource Hierarchy for Learning Hidden Structure in Diffusion Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract We study score learning from denoising pairs with a hidden non-Gaussian
component. In one regime covariance reveals it; in another, isotropic
covariance hides it until the first distinguishing moment, of order k ∗ k^{\ast} .
Denoising-loss correlations are Stein discrepancies against a baseline
and, for polynomial fields, exactly encode moment differences.
Averaging noisy views of each clean point gives exact moment queries. In the covariance-matched regime, orientation-independent dictionaries
satisfying an L 4 / L 2 L^{4}/L^{2} condition need order d k ∗ − 1 d^{k^{\ast}-1} features.
The stated dot-product kernel ridge models need the same power in samples,
as does small-step online SGD on one unit up to logarithms. A two-stage
learner uses Gaussian-smoothed-loss curvature to recover the direction,
then sharpens it and fits a scalar readout. For even k ∗ k^{\ast} ,
it obtains a fixed score gain over the Gaussian baseline from O ⁡ ( d k ∗ / 2 ​ log ⁡ d ) O(d^{k^{\ast}/2}\log d) clean points. In the covariance-visible regime,
the frozen-feature threshold is d J / J ! d^{J}/J! ; projection onto principal
components makes fitted-model, score-risk, and generated-law distributions
independent of ambient dimension. Experiments are consistent with the spectral transition. A width-8 network
trained with clean-point reuse shows a d 2 d^{2} -like
training-set threshold over d = 64 d=64 – 192 192 , with fixed validation and
calibration overhead.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models estimate the score ∇ log ⁡ p t \nabla\log p_{t} as Gaussian noise progressively obscures a data distribution ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . Training provides denoising pairs ( X 0 , X t ) (X_{0},X_{t}) : a clean point and a noisy view. The learner predicts X 0 X_{0} from X t X_{t} , thereby estimating the score ( Vincent, 2011 ) . If the data have a hidden non-Gaussian direction, a successful denoiser must detect it through those pairs. The amount of data needed depends on what the learner can represent and whether it can use repeated views of the same clean point. Existing theory studies parts of this question under different data models and resource measures. Lower bounds for random features and kernels count features or samples for fixed representations ( Ghorbani et al., 2021 ; Mei et al., 2022 ) ; analyses of trained denoisers count fresh pairs for one architecture and optimizer ( Bardone et al., 2026 ) ; statistical-query and cryptographic lower bounds count queries or computation for arbitrary algorithms ( Diakonikolas et al., 2017 ; Song, 2024 ) . These results do not directly compare the cost of learning the same hidden signal across learner classes. We ask: Which moments of a hidden structure can a denoising learner access, and how do representation size, distinct clean samples, noisy views and the learner’s access to geometry determine the cost of improving on the Gaussian score? We study two versions of one hidden-component model. Data are X 0 = U ​ Z + σ 0 ​ ( I − U ​ U ⊤ ) ​ G 0 X_{0}=UZ+\sigma_{0}(I-UU^{\top})G_{0} with an unknown orthonormal U ∈ ℝ d × k U\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} , a non-Gaussian latent vector Z ∈ ℝ k Z\in\mathbb{R}^{k} and an independent Gaussian G 0 G_{0} . In the covariance-visible regime ( σ 0 = 0 \sigma_{0}=0 ), the data lie on the subspace, their covariance reveals U U , and principal components recover it from k + 1 k+1 points. In the covariance-matched regime, Cov ⁡ ( Z ) = σ 0 2 ​ I k \mathrm{Cov}(Z)=\sigma_{0}^{2}I_{k} , so Cov ⁡ ( X 0 ) = σ 0 2 ​ I d \mathrm{Cov}(X_{0})=\sigma_{0}^{2}I_{d} carries no information about U U . The first informative moment has order k ∗ ≥ 3 k^{\ast}\geq 3 , the generative exponent of the latent law. This is non-Gaussian component analysis ( Diakonikolas et al., 2017 ; Tan and Vershynin, 2018 ) seen through a diffusion model.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: The Stein–Tweedie identity expresses each residual correlation as a discrepancy between the noisy law and a baseline (Theorem 3.1 ); on polynomial fields, these correlations recover exactly the corresponding moment differences (Theorem 3.2 ). Thus a fitted Gaussian baseline removes the moments it matches, shifting the first accessible signal in the covariance-visible mixture from degree two to degree four (Theorem 3.4 , Corollary 3.6 ). Conditioning on the clean point gives an exact clean-data moment query (Lemma 3.3 ). Averaging fresh noisy views of one point reduces the forward-process variance of the corresponding gradient estimate. Diffusion acts on the hidden coordinate through an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck noise operator; the static signal-to-noise ratio of the best low-degree correlation peaks at the time in Theorem 3.8 . For an orientation-independent dictionary, the covariance-visible mixture has a sharp feature threshold at d 3 / 6 d^{3}/6 , with higher odd-degree steps at d J / J ! d^{J}/J! (Theorems 4.5 , 4.9 ). For one hidden direction, a one-sided change of measure identifies the height of the first step (Theorem 4.13 ). The covariance-matched model gives the d k ∗ − 1 d^{k^{\ast}-1} exponent for dictionaries satisfying the stated L 4 / L 2 L^{4}/L^{2} condition (Theorem 4.21 ). Kernel ridge regression on noisy inputs has the same sample exponent under the conditions of Theorem 5.2 ; for the exponential kernel this includes every ridge (Lemma 5.3 ). When covariance reveals the subspace, principal-component projection instead yields fitted-model, score-risk and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension (Theorems 4.15 , 4.16 ). Learning the covariance-matched direction can be cheaper than fixing a representation in advance. Small-step online SGD on one unit needs d k ∗ − 1 d^{k^{\ast}-1} steps up to log 2 ⁡ d \log^{2}d (Corollary 6.2 ), while the statistical-query bound gives tolerance d − k ∗ / 4 + o ( 1 ) d^{-k^{\ast}/4+o(1)} under its output-norm assumption (Proposition 6.3 ). Averaging r r noisy views of each clean point, one gradient step of the matrix score model recovers the direction from O ⁡ ( ( 1 + ( ι t − 1 ) / r ) ​ d k ∗ / 2 ​ log ⁡ d ) O((1+(\iota_{t}-1)/r)d^{k^{\ast}/2}\log d) clean points for even k ∗ k^{\ast} (Theorem 6.5 ). The same partial-trace matrix is the curvature created by Gaussian smoothing of a single-unit loss (Proposition 6.7 ). A learner that uses this curvature, sharpens the direction and fits a scalar readout obtains a fixed score gain with O ⁡ ( d k ∗ / 2 ​ log ⁡ d ) + O ⁡ ( d ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(d^{k^{\ast}/2}\log d)+O(d)+O(1) clean points (Theorem 6.8 ). For k ∗ = 4 k^{\ast}=4 , this separates it from the restricted learner classes above by one power of d d , up to logarithms and under their stated hypotheses (Corollary 6.9 ). The experiments check the predicted barriers and invariances in the covariance-visible regime. In the covariance-matched regime, the partial trace’s measured overlaps are consistent with the proposed spectral transition within Monte Carlo error. A width-8 network trained with clean-point reuse has a d 2 d^{2} -like training-set threshold over d = 64 d=64 – 192 192 , with fixed validation and calibration overhead (Section 7 ).

sections.heading: Low-dimensional structure in diffusion models.
sections.text: Chen et al. (2023a) give score approximation and estimation rates for data on a linear subspace, Oko et al. (2023) prove minimax optimality of diffusion estimators over Besov classes, and Li and Yan (2024) show that samplers adapt to unknown intrinsic dimension. Given an accurate score, sampling error is controlled by Chen et al. (2023b) and Benton et al. (2024) . These are upper bounds for adaptive estimators; our lower bounds identify what restricted classes lack, and our upper bounds count each resource separately.

sections.heading: Fixed representations and kernels.
sections.text: Random-feature and kernel models in high dimension fit only polynomial components of degree ℓ \ell with d ℓ ≪ N d^{\ell}\ll N features or samples ( Ghorbani et al., 2019 ; Ghorbani et al., 2021 ; Mei et al., 2022 ) , and the spectrum of inner-product kernel matrices in polynomial regimes is described by Misiakiewicz (2022) and Lu and Yau (2022) . For denoising score matching, George et al. (2026) derive precise learning curves for random features and George and Macris (2026) extend them to manifold data. Here the inputs are non-Gaussian along a hidden direction, and the barrier applies to every orientation-blind dictionary with arbitrary coefficients. For one hidden direction, it also gives the exact risk height relative to the moment-matched Gaussian denoiser.

sections.heading: Exponents, statistical queries and non-Gaussian component analysis.
sections.text: The information exponent governs online SGD for single-index models ( Ben Arous et al., 2021 ) , and the generative exponent governs statistical-query and low-degree algorithms ( Damian et al., 2024 ) . Statistical-query lower bounds for non-Gaussian component analysis are due to Diakonikolas et al. (2017) and Diakonikolas et al. (2024) , spectral algorithms to Vempala and Xiao (2011) and Tan and Vershynin (2018) , and score estimation for such data is cryptographically hard in general ( Song, 2024 ) . Bardone et al. (2026) show that a denoiser trained online on a mixed cumulant model learns pair-wise statistics at linear cost and the fourth cumulant at cubic cost, defining a diffusion information exponent; Székely et al. (2024) report a quadratic sample threshold for supervised networks in a spiked cumulant model. Our Theorem 3.2 identifies the generative exponent as the relevant one for denoising, and Corollary 3.6 gives a mechanism for the staged learning of Bardone et al. (2026) .

sections.heading: Tensor methods, smoothing and reuse.
sections.text: The fourth-moment tensor of non-Gaussian component data is a spiked tensor, for which unfolding reaches d k / 2 d^{k/2} ( Montanari and Richard, 2014 ) and gradient descent or Langevin dynamics from random starts needs d k − 1 d^{k-1} ( Ben Arous et al., 2020 ) . Gaussian smoothing reaches the unfolding threshold for tensor PCA ( Anandkumar et al., 2017 ) and the d k / 2 d^{k/2} rate for online single-index learning ( Damian et al., 2023 ) ; SGD can be viewed as optimizing a smoothed objective ( Kleinberg et al., 2018 ) . Reusing batches changes what gradient methods can learn in supervised two-layer networks ( Dandi et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) . A link between one gradient step of a diffusion objective and a spectral method was made for a covariance spike by Shah et al. (2023) . Here the conditional Stein identity connects reuse to the denoising loss, and the curvature created by smoothing is the partial-trace statistic. The resulting two-stage learner has explicit costs for clean points, noisy views and arithmetic.

sections.heading: Stein’s method and score matching.
sections.text: Theorem 3.1 is a standard consequence of Stein’s lemma and Tweedie’s formula ( Robbins, 1956 ; Efron, 2011 ) ; its supremum over a unit ball of fields is a Stein discrepancy ( Gorham and Mackey, 2015 ) , and the equivalence of denoising score matching with score matching is due to Hyvärinen (2005) and Vincent (2011) . We use this identity to compare what different denoising learners can extract from the same hidden-component model.

sections.heading: 2.3 Learners and the resources they spend
sections.text: We track four resources separately. • Representation size M M : the dimension of a frozen dictionary. • Distinct clean points : the total budget counts training, selection (validation) and readout (calibration) points. Theorems state every part explicitly (for example n 1 n_{1} , n 2 n_{2} , n 3 n_{3} in Theorem 6.8 ). In the experiments, n n denotes the training-set size; every learner there also uses one fixed set of 32,768 32{,}768 validation and one of 32,768 32{,}768 calibration points, independent of n n , and the tables report this overhead next to each training-set threshold. • Noisy presentations : the total number of views ( x 0 , a t ​ x 0 + h t ​ g ) (x_{0},a_{t}x_{0}+\sqrt{h_{t}}\,g) used, with r r views per clean point under reuse; views of one clean point share x 0 x_{0} and use independent g g . • Computation : arithmetic operations, reported where relevant. A d 3 d^{3} barrier on dictionary size M M imposes no d 3 d^{3} lower bound on clean points n n . An algorithm using d 2 d^{2} clean points may require many more noisy presentations. Definition 2.1 (Orientation-independent dictionary) . A dictionary is a random linear space 𝒮 = 𝒮 ⁡ ( ω ) \mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}(\omega) of measurable functions ℝ d → ℝ \mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} , of dimension at most M M , where ω \omega is a random element whose law does not depend on U U and which is independent of U U when U U is random. An estimator m ^ ​ ( ⋅ , t ) \widehat{m}(\cdot,t) is supported by 𝒮 \mathcal{S} if, almost surely, every coordinate function x ↦ e i ⊤ ​ m ^ ​ ( x , t ) x\mapsto e_{i}^{\top}\widehat{m}(x,t) lies in 𝒮 + 𝒜 \mathcal{S}+\mathcal{A} , where 𝒜 = span ⁡ { 1 , x 1 , … , x d } \mathcal{A}=\spanop\{1,x_{1},\dots,x_{d}\} . The element ω \omega may contain random weights, the latent training samples, auxiliary seeds and any rotation-invariant statistic of the training inputs; it may not contain the orientation. The coefficients that combine dictionary elements, the affine part, the output directions and any selection among candidates may all depend on the data and on U U . Selecting among several dictionaries is covered by their sum. We assume that 𝒮 \mathcal{S} is spanned by finitely many random functions that are jointly measurable in ( ω , x ) (\omega,x) .

sections.heading: Gradient learners.
sections.text: A gradient learner fits a parametric correction f θ f_{\theta} by descending the empirical denoising loss L ^ ​ ( θ ) = ‖ x 0 − m t Q ​ ( x t ) − f θ ​ ( x t ) ‖ 2 ¯ \widehat{L}(\theta)=\overline{\|x_{0}-m^{Q}_{t}(x_{t})-f_{\theta}(x_{t})\|^{2}} , the bar denoting an average over the views used. Online learners draw a fresh clean point and a fresh view at each step; reuse learners revisit n n stored clean points with fresh views; full-batch learners average over all views at once. Corollary 3.5 (Exact polynomial barrier) . Under Assumption 3 with the isotropic baseline, the best approximation in L 2 ​ ( P t ) L^{2}(P_{t}) of m t − m t Q m_{t}-m^{Q}_{t} by polynomial fields of degree at most k ∗ − 2 k^{\ast}-2 is zero. No polynomial dictionary of degree below k ∗ − 1 k^{\ast}-1 , of any size, improves the score on the Gaussian baseline, at any orientation, dimension or time. Corollary 3.6 (Gaussian preconditioning shifts the exponent) . Suppose P 0 P_{0} has an anisotropic covariance with range U U , as in Assumption 2 . Against an isotropic baseline the first moment mismatch is at order two, and correlations with linear fields reveal U U . Against the Gaussian fitted to the first two moments, correlations with fields of degree at most one vanish; if the latent law is centrally symmetric, those of degree two vanish as well; and if its fourth cumulant tensor is nonzero (for the two-component mixture it is − 2 ​ μ 4 -2\mu^{4} per coordinate), the first nonzero correlation has degree three and the exponent is four. Corollary 3.6 is the mechanism behind the two regimes. In the covariance-visible regime the Gaussian part of the score teaches the geometry: correlations of degree one reveal the subspace at linear cost. A learner that subtracts the fitted Gaussian, or a frozen representation that cannot use the covariance, faces exponent four, and Section 4 shows that it pays a cubic price. It also explains the staged learning observed by Bardone et al. (2026) : once a model has fitted the Gaussian part of the score, the correlations it can still exploit are of order at least three.

sections.heading: 7 Experiments
sections.text: The experiments measure risk barriers, dimension invariance, threshold locations and leading constants. For each study, we fixed the prediction, statistic and decision rule in a tracked protocol before collecting data. We report every pre-stated outcome, including the failed predictions in Section 7.3 . Appendix E gives the protocols, hardware, seeds and record definitions.

sections.heading: 7.1 Covariance-visible regime
sections.text: All runs use Assumption 2 with μ = 1.5 \mu=1.5 , τ = 0.35 \tau=0.35 , r = 8 r=8 corruptions per example, ridge grid { 10 − 6 , … , 10 − 1 } \{10^{-6},\dots,10^{-1}\} and L = 3 L=3 bandwidths, with selection on held-out denoising error only. Ambient, PCA and oracle methods share weights, data and corruption noise within a replicate, and each replicate draws a fresh Haar orientation. Score risks are Monte Carlo averages against exact population scores (Lemma 4.2 ). The main suite has 168 units (barrier, feature budget, certificate, generation) and ran on one Tesla T4 in 4.9 4.9 GPU-hours; the revision suite has 60 units (staircase, data off the subspace, generation off the subspace) and ran on a 16-core CPU. The pre-stated checks were: (i) no detected barrier violation, (ii) PCA and oracle denoisers equal to floating-point precision with noiseless data, (iii) PCA risk and W 2 W_{2} invariant in d d up to Monte Carlo error, (iv) zero off-subspace mass, and (v) the full level- J J Hermite dictionary at the dimension-free level k ​ ( a t / h t ) 2 ​ ε J ​ ( t ) k(a_{t}/h_{t})^{2}\varepsilon_{J}(t) at every d d . All five hold in the tested configurations.

sections.heading: Barrier and invariance.
sections.text: No cell of the barrier study (288 cells) falls more than three standard errors below the Ky Fan floor. PCA and oracle fitted denoisers differ by at most 3.8 × 10 − 12 3.8\times 10^{-12} , and the PCA risk varies across d ∈ { 8 , … , 256 } d\in\{8,\dots,256\} with maximal | z | = 3.12 |z|=3.12 over all configurations. At t = 0.3 t=0.3 the PCA risk stays near 0.003 0.003 for every d d , while the ambient risk rises to the Gaussian control’s value, about 0.52 0.52 , once d ≥ 64 d\geq 64 , even with p = 1024 p=1024 features.

sections.heading: Staircase.
sections.text: In the best-in-span study, none of 324 cells falls below the floor. The full cubic Hermite dictionary reaches the predicted dimension-free level within 8 % 8\% at every d ∈ { 6 , … , 32 } d\in\{6,\dots,32\} (dimensions 63 63 to 6017 6017 ), and the quintic dictionary reaches ε 5 \varepsilon_{5} within 5 % 5\% . Normalized by N d , 3 N_{d,3} , the curves at t ∈ { 0.6 , 1 } t\in\{0.6,1\} coincide across d d (Figure 7 ); tanh random features of equal size stay four to six times above the cubic level at t = 1 t=1 . The approach to the cubic level is convex in M / N d , 3 M/N_{d,3} , so the explicit barrier is conservative in shape but exact in location.

sections.heading: Exact height.
sections.text: Theorem 4.13 , in its Ky Fan form and with the time change of Proposition 4.14 off the subspace, was checked against all 1116 cells with k = 1 k=1 . The number of cells more than three standard errors below the bound is 0; the bound exceeds the cubic floor of Theorem 4.5 in 265 cells and reaches up to 99% of the measured risk. For the ambient estimator at d ≥ 64 d\geq 64 and t ≥ 0.6 t\geq 0.6 (30 cells) it lies between 32% and 98% of the measured risk, so the failure of geometry-blind features to improve on the Gaussian control is largely accounted for by the bound.

sections.heading: Network sample scaling (X4).
sections.text: The X4 study asks how many distinct clean points a gradient-trained network needs. Its learner, frozen in advance, is a width-8 network of units He 3 ​ ( w j ⊤ ​ x ) ​ v j \mathrm{He}_{3}(w_{j}^{\top}x)\,v_{j} with normalized first-layer weights, trained by minibatch SGD (batch 512, 16 ​ d 2 16d^{2} steps, learning rate 0.1 0.1 or 0.3 0.3 selected on validation) that cycles over n n clean points with fresh noise. At 32 checkpoints a tied readout, one coefficient per unit, is fitted on 32,768 32{,}768 calibration pairs and the checkpoint is selected by readout-fitted loss on 32,768 32{,}768 validation pairs. A run succeeds if its test gain is at least 0.25 0.25 of B B ; n 50 ​ ( d ) n_{50}(d) is the 50% point of a penalized logistic fit over a 15-point grid n / d 2 ∈ [ 0.5 , 64 ] n/d^{2}\in[0.5,64] with eight seeds, and the pre-stated decision was H2 ( n 50 ∝ d 2 n_{50}\propto d^{2} ) if the slope of log ⁡ n 50 \log n_{50} on log ⁡ d \log d was at most 2.4 2.4 with upper 95% limit below 2.7 2.7 , and H3 ( ∝ d 3 \propto d^{3} ) if at least 2.6 2.6 with lower limit above 2.3 2.3 . The pre-registered heuristic favoured H3: small-step reuse descends a fixed landscape whose correlation part is tensor PCA, for which local methods need d 3 d^{3} ( Ben Arous et al., 2020 ) . The GPU study (1,080 cells, d ∈ { 64,128,192 } d\in\{64,128,192\} ) returned H2: slope 1.84 1.84 (the frozen protocol’s seed bootstrap gives a 95% interval 1.50 1.50 – 2.17 2.17 , the cell bootstrap below 1.48 1.48 – 2.18 2.18 ), with no failure to escape at the top of the grid. Over this factor-of-three range in dimension, the threshold follows a d 2 d^{2} -like trend. The asymptotic exponent remains unresolved.

sections.heading: What is counted.
sections.text: Here n n is the size of the training set. Each run also uses 32,768 32{,}768 validation and 32,768 32{,}768 calibration pairs, drawn once for each ( d , seed ) (d,\text{seed}) and shared by every n n and both learning rates; under the accounting of Section 2.3 these are clean points too. They amount to 16.0 16.0 , 4.0 4.0 and 1.78 ​ d 2 1.78\,d^{2} at d = 64,128,192 d=64,128,192 (Table 4 ), so the network’s total budget at its threshold is 18.7 18.7 , 6.8 6.8 and 4.0 ​ d 2 4.0\,d^{2} : in this range the fixed overhead dominates at small d d , and the total budget per d 2 d^{2} falls with d d . All d 2 d^{2} statements of this section therefore concern the training-set threshold at a fixed overhead, and all comparisons are between learners given the same overhead and the same success rule. Asymptotically the overhead is of lower order (Theorem 6.8 needs n 2 = O ⁡ ( d ) n_{2}=O(d) and n 3 = O ⁡ ( 1 ) n_{3}=O(1) ), but these experiments do not reach that regime. Thresholds carry 95% intervals from a cell bootstrap: the eight outcomes of each ( d , n ) (d,n) cell are resampled, 2,000 times, and the threshold fit is repeated. The cell bootstrap is exact for the explicit learners, whose runs use independent randomness; for the GPU arm it ignores the coupling of runs that share a seed across n n . Contrasts (Table 5 ) are ratios of independently resampled thresholds.

sections.heading: The explicit learners.
sections.text: We ran the learner of Theorem 6.8 on the identical protocol and overhead: stage 1 on the n n training points, sharpening on the 32,768 32{,}768 validation points, and the same tied readout on the 32,768 32{,}768 calibration points, with the same success rule and threshold fit. Full reuse is computed directly as the clean partial trace M p ​ ( x 0 ) M_{p}(x_{0}) (Section 6 , Presentations under reuse ), at the arithmetic cost of one view and with no noisy presentations; the sharpening step with full reuse uses the corresponding clean statistic. Table 4 and Figure 8 (b,c) report the thresholds. Every learner run with the standard overhead has slope between 1.84 1.84 and 2.15 2.15 , each interval within 1.48 1.48 – 2.39 2.39 . The constants order as the theory predicts. Learners that use the clean statistic sit within a factor of about two of the reuse transition n c = 2.98 ​ d 2 n_{c}=2.98\,d^{2} , and the ratio of one-view to full-reuse thresholds is 2.27 2.27 – 2.59 2.59 for the two-stage learners and 2.13 2.13 – 2.82 2.82 for the spectral-only learners, against the predicted inflation ι t ∗ = 64 / 27 ≈ 2.37 \iota_{t^{\ast}}=64/27\approx 2.37 of Theorem 6.5 ; five of the six intervals contain it. The CPU replication of the single-view spectral learner ( 33 33 – 36 ​ d 2 36\,d^{2} ) agrees with the frozen GPU arm ( 30 30 – 33 ​ d 2 33\,d^{2} ), with overlapping intervals. Spectral-only learners need an overlap high enough for the readout to clear the gain threshold, about 1 − n c / n ≥ 0.8 1-n_{c}/n\geq 0.8 , which multiplies their thresholds by about five. One sharpening step, the learner analysed in Theorem 6.8 , lowers the full-reuse threshold from 12.6 12.6 – 15.5 ​ d 2 15.5\,d^{2} to 5.0 5.0 – 6.3 ​ d 2 6.3\,d^{2} , and three steps to 3.7 3.7 – 4.3 ​ d 2 4.3\,d^{2} , as the theorem’s separation of geometry from accuracy predicts.

sections.heading: Sensitivity to the overhead.
sections.text: Sharpening spends the validation set. With 8,192 8{,}192 validation and 8,192 8{,}192 calibration points (rows marked † \dagger ), the one-step learner needs 7.7 7.7 , 10.9 10.9 and 15.3 ​ d 2 15.3\,d^{2} training points, 1.3 1.3 – 2.4 2.4 times as many as with the standard overhead, and the ratio grows with d d (slope 2.61 2.61 , interval 2.43 2.43 – 2.80 2.80 ). This is the trade-off of the proof of Theorem 6.8 : the sharpening budget scales as d d divided by a power of the stage-1 overlap, so a sharpening set that shrinks relative to d d , from 128 ​ d 128d to 43 ​ d 43d , must be paid for with a better stage-1 direction and hence more training points. At these dimensions the sample cost of the explicit learner is its total budget n + n 2 + n 3 n+n_{2}+n_{3} , not n n alone, and its d 2 d^{2} slope is a statement at a fixed, ample overhead.

sections.heading: The trained network.
sections.text: Under the common success rule and validation overhead, the SGD-trained network needs 2.2 2.2 – 2.8 ​ d 2 2.8\,d^{2} training points. Its thresholds are 0.35 0.35 – 0.57 0.57 of those of the one-step two-stage learner, with bootstrap intervals excluding one at every d d , and 0.51 0.51 – 0.77 0.77 of those of the three-step learner; the latter interval reaches one at d = 128 d=128 (Table 5 ). The network also needs roughly an order of magnitude fewer training points than the single-view spectral step. For the learners tested here, the network thresholds lie at 0.73 0.73 – 0.95 0.95 of n c n_{c} , but n c n_{c} marks the overlap transition of the clean partial-trace eigenvector, rather than a denoising-gain threshold. The methods also use their fixed validation and calibration sets differently: the network selects among 64 checkpoints and learning rates and fits an eight-coefficient readout; the two-stage learner uses these points to sharpen its direction. The network’s sensitivity to a smaller overhead has not been measured. At its threshold, the network processes 16 ​ d 2 × 512 = 8,192 ​ d 2 16d^{2}\times 512=8{,}192\,d^{2} noisy presentations, or 2,900 2{,}900 – 3,800 3{,}800 views per clean point. Its clean-sample result is therefore measured in a high-reuse regime. Conjecture 6.5 asks whether SGD forms the smoothed curvature of Proposition 6.7 . sections.heading: The earlier X4 screens.
sections.text: Before the two-stage protocol, an uncalibrated version that used the network’s own output layer passed the gain threshold in 2 / 3 2/3 seeds at d = 64 d=64 but in 0 / 3 0/3 at d = 96 d=96 and 128 128 . A diagnostic that refitted a tied readout on independent pairs raised the d = 128 d=128 gains to 0.71 0.71 in 3 / 3 3/3 seeds: the first layers had aligned, and the output layer was the bottleneck. This motivated the two-stage protocol, frozen before the rate study.

sections.heading: Diffusion time in fixed-step SGD (X1).
sections.text: We trained a single Hermite-3 unit by spherical online SGD with step 0.1 / d 0.1/d , using sixteen paired seeds per ( d , t ) (d,t) over seven times. The pre-stated prediction was that the escape time scales as S t − 2 S_{t}^{-2} : fastest time in [ 0.10 , 0.20 ] [0.10,0.20] , and a t = 0.6 t=0.6 to t ∗ t^{\ast} ratio in [ 3.5 , 8 ] [3.5,8] . The fastest time was in the interval at d = 32 d=32 and d = 64 d=64 , but the ratio was 7.77 7.77 at d = 32 d=32 and 32.37 32.37 at d = 64 d=64 (bootstrap interval 10.2 10.2 – 75.9 75.9 ), which falsifies the ratio prediction for this optimizer. The fixed step falls outside the small-step regime of Corollary 6.2 . Theorem 3.8 concerns a static signal-to-noise ratio, while Theorem 6.5 (5) gives the time result for the analysed spectral learner.

sections.heading: Residual exponent for fixed-step SGD (X2).
sections.text: In the covariance-visible model, we ran paired spherical SGD with the full target and with the fitted-Gaussian residual. The full arm escaped after about d ​ log ⁡ d d\log d pairs, as predicted. The residual arm was predicted to need d 3 d^{3} ; its fitted exponent over d ∈ { 16 , … , 128 } d\in\{16,\dots,128\} was 1.57 1.57 (interval 1.37 1.37 – 2.26 2.26 ), below the cutoff 2.5 2.5 . Corollary 3.6 concerns the degree of the first nonzero population correlation, not a finite-step escape exponent, and the residual arm was calibrated from a clean point that reveals the span exactly, so the experiment tests the gradient signal of the residual parametrization rather than a best-algorithm sample complexity.

sections.heading: Gradient descent on the unsmoothed reuse landscape.
sections.text: Deterministic gradient descent on the noise-averaged single-unit landscape, with the output coefficient profiled out, from eight random starts on each of three data sets per ( d , n ) (d,n) , did not reach 50% escape by n = 64 ​ d 2 n=64d^{2} at any d ∈ { 32 , 64 , 128 } d\in\{32,64,128\} ( 11 / 24 11/24 , 5 / 24 5/24 and 10 / 24 10/24 starts escaped at the top of the grid), while the single-view spectral statistic on the same clean points reached squared overlap 0.88 0.88 – 0.89 0.89 . This is consistent with Proposition 6.7 , which shows that the unsmoothed landscape is flat to third order at the origin, and with the d 3 d^{3} threshold of local methods for tensor PCA ( Ben Arous et al., 2020 ) .

sections.heading: 8 Discussion
sections.text: The gradient of the denoising loss exposes moment differences between the data and a baseline (Theorem 3.2 ). A polynomial field of degree below k ∗ − 1 k^{\ast}-1 cannot use the first unmatched moment (Corollary 3.5 ). Under the hypotheses of Theorems 4.21 and 5.2 and Corollary 6.2 , frozen dictionaries, kernel ridge regression and small-step online training of one unit pay d k ∗ − 1 d^{k^{\ast}-1} in their respective resources. In the covariance-visible regime the frozen threshold is exactly at d 3 / 6 d^{3}/6 ; for one hidden direction, its first-step height is the Gaussian control (Theorems 4.9 and 4.13 ). The two-stage learner forms the curvature of a smoothed denoising landscape and averages over noisy views of each clean point. It needs O ⁡ ( d k ∗ / 2 ​ log ⁡ d ) O(d^{k^{\ast}/2}\log d) clean points (Theorem 6.8 ). Proposition 6.3 gives a statistical-query tolerance bound of d − k ∗ / 4 d^{-k^{\ast}/4} , but does not prove a matching sample lower bound for gradient learners. When covariance reveals the subspace, a fitted Gaussian baseline and principal components give a projected estimator whose risk law is independent of ambient dimension (Corollary 3.6 , Theorem 4.15 ). Averaging fresh noisy views of one clean point removes the forward-process variance in the analysed learner. The learner uses more presentations of each point without requiring more clean points (Lemma 3.3 , Theorem 6.5 ). For one view per point, the leading spectral constant is minimized at t ∗ t^{\ast} ; full reuse removes this time-dependent inflation. Once the learner has found the direction, fitting a scalar readout on independent pairs turns alignment into a score gain at dimension-free sample cost (Theorem 6.8 ). In the X4 study, output-layer calibration affected the measured gain even when the first layer was aligned. The two-stage theorem covers one hidden direction and even k ∗ k^{\ast} . Its learner uses strong smoothing, equivalently a matrix parameter, and independent data splits. The clean-sample bound includes a logarithm and, for k ∗ > 4 k^{\ast}>4 , a non-sharp constant. The proof does not cover standard network training. The covariance-matched frozen-feature theorem assumes an L 4 / L 2 L^{4}/L^{2} constant that has not been established for random-feature spans. The kernel theorem assumes a high-degree Taylor coefficient. The exact-height result covers the first staircase step for one hidden direction. PCA invariance uses noiseless training points; off-subspace degradation is measured here but has no bound in the current analysis. We do not derive a lower bound on generated-sample error. Spectral experiments end at d = 256 d=256 , and the trained-network study ends at d = 192 d=192 .

sections.heading: Guide to the appendices
sections.text: The appendices are organized by proof technique. This guide lists the results, their dependencies and the notation used in the proofs. Roadmaps at the start of each appendix and long proof indicate the order of the arguments.

sections.heading: How the results depend on each other
sections.text: Two lemmas carry most of the weight. Lemma 4.4 (an orientation-averaged Ky Fan bound) drives every frozen-feature lower bound in both regimes, and Lemma 3.3 (the conditional Stein identity) drives every positive training result. The one-sided change of measure (Lemma 4.12 ) is the bridge that turns the covariance-visible argument into the covariance-matched one.

Roadmap: how Appendix B is organized 1. Reductions ( B.1 – B.3 ): the score problem becomes a one-dimensional regression of the posterior mean g t g_{t} , and the data density is compared with the orientation-free reference γ \gamma . 2. Spectral core ( B.4 ): the orientation-averaged captured energy of any M M -dimensional span is a Ky Fan sum of a Funk–Hecke spectrum; this is the engine of every lower bound. 3. Cubic barrier and its refinements ( B.5 – B.9 ): average over orientations, then every orientation for isotropic features, typical orientations by concentration on the sphere, and sharpness by explicit polynomial dictionaries. 4. Exact height ( B.10 – B.11 ): the one-sided change of measure removes the density factor from the main term. 5. Robustness and the adaptive side ( B.12 – B.16 ): time change for data off the subspace, monotonicity in d d , and the exact dimension invariance of the PCA estimator and its sampler.

sections.heading: Appendix C Proofs for the covariance-matched frozen and kernel results
sections.text: Roadmap: how Appendix C is organized Both barriers in the covariance-matched regime bound the correlation between the hidden residual and what the learner can represent. For frozen dictionaries ( C.1 – C.2 ) the representation is fixed before the orientation, so the one-sided change of measure of Appendix B applies, with hypercontractivity (Lemma 4.20 ) replacing the density floor that does not exist here. For kernels ( C.3 – C.5 ) the span depends on the data, so the argument instead bounds the leakage of the residual onto each kernel section (Lemma 5.1 ) and the size of the coefficients, through the ridge or through the smallest eigenvalue of the high-degree kernel matrix (Lemma 5.3 ).

sections.text: Roadmap: how Appendix D is organized 1. Lower side for one unit ( D.1 – D.2 ): the population loss of one unit is a polynomial in the overlap with information exponent k ∗ k^{\ast} , so the online SGD theory of Ben Arous et al. sections.heading: E.2 Covariance-matched studies
sections.text: The covariance-matched studies used the following designs. • X3 : nested quadratic Hermite dictionaries, ridge fits on 4,096 pairs, 32,768 test pairs, eight seeds, Holm-corrected one-sided tests. • X5 : exponential-kernel ridge regression on noisy inputs, d ∈ { 8 , 11 , 16 } d\in\{8,11,16\} , n ≤ 2 ​ d 3 n\leq 2d^{3} , ridges 10 − 8 10^{-8} – 10 2 10^{2} , three seeds; eigenvalue study to d = 512 d=512 . • Spectral statistics : single-view recovery curves in units of v t ​ d 2 / κ ¯ t 2 v_{t}d^{2}/\bar{\kappa}_{t}^{2} , four seeds; clean partial-trace overlaps at n = x ⋅ 2 ​ d 2 / κ 4 2 n=x\cdot 2d^{2}/\kappa_{4}^{2} , x ∈ { 0.5 , … , 8 } x\in\{0.5,\dots,8\} , d ∈ { 64,128,256 } d\in\{64,128,256\} , eight seeds. • X4 rate study : 1,080 cells on two RTX 4090 GPUs under the second, frozen protocol. The archived run records have a recorded SHA-256 digest. • Two-stage learner on the X4 protocol : identical grid, seeds, budgets, success rule and threshold fit; variants r ∈ { 1 , ∞ } r\in\{1,\infty\} with zero, one or three sharpening steps on the validation split, and a sensitivity run of the one-step full-reuse variant with 8,192-point validation and calibration sets. • X1, X2 and the landscape study : the online, preconditioning and reuse comparisons described in Section 7 . The identities of Lemma 3.3 , Theorem 6.5 (1,3) and Proposition 6.7 were also checked by Monte Carlo.

sections.heading: Auditing the covariance-matched numbers.
sections.text: Each covariance-matched protocol was fixed before its study ran. The replicate-level records of the explicit learners retain the variant, validation and calibration size, dimension, training size, seed, normalized gain and squared overlaps. A run succeeds when its normalized gain is at least 0.25 0.25 . Spectral-transition records contain one row per run. The X4 thresholds and intervals use per-cell success counts; full run histories are archived with a recorded digest. The sensitivity run reduces each of the validation and calibration sets to 8,192 8{,}192 points.

sections.text: No Gaussian-control or ambient cell falls below the time-changed Ky Fan floor of Proposition 4.14 by more than three standard errors ( 0 0 of 384 384 ), and with σ 0 = 0 \sigma_{0}=0 the PCA risks again vary across d d only within Monte Carlo error (largest standardized deviation 2.4 2.4 ). The measured ‖ sin ⁡ Θ ‖ F 2 \left\lVert\sin\Theta\right\rVert_{F}^{2} agrees with the spiked-covariance reference once d ≥ 32 d\geq 32 (Table 13 ). Ambient random features show no measurable improvement over the Gaussian control once d ≥ 128 d\geq 128 , at every σ 0 \sigma_{0} , n n and t t . With σ 0 > 0 \sigma_{0}>0 every method’s risk grows with d d at fixed n n , because the shared baseline estimates a d d -dimensional mean and an off-subspace variance from noisy data. This growth is common to the Gaussian control, the PCA estimator and the oracle-projection estimator: PCA and oracle risks differ by a median of 1.3 % 1.3\% over the 144 144 cells with σ 0 > 0 \sigma_{0}>0 , and coincide at σ 0 = 0 \sigma_{0}=0 . The part of the risk that the barrier concerns, the improvement over the Gaussian control, is nearly independent of d d . At t = 0.3 t=0.3 the PCA estimator’s absolute improvement varies by at most 13 % 13\% of its d = 8 d=8 value across d ∈ { 8 , … , 512 } d\in\{8,\dots,512\} for σ 0 ≤ 0.3 \sigma_{0}\leq 0.3 at every n n , and for σ 0 = 1 \sigma_{0}=1 it stays within 20 % 20\% of its d = 8 d=8 value while d ​ σ 0 2 / n ≤ 1 / 8 d\sigma_{0}^{2}/n\leq 1/8 . It collapses once d ​ σ 0 2 / n ≥ 1 / 2 d\sigma_{0}^{2}/n\geq 1/2 , where ‖ sin ⁡ Θ ‖ F 2 ≥ 0.23 \left\lVert\sin\Theta\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq 0.23 : there the PCA estimator retains at most a quarter of its d = 8 d=8 improvement, while the oracle projection retains 30 30 – 80 % 80\% . This is the only regime in the grid in which subspace estimation, rather than feature learning or the baseline, limits the adaptive estimator. Every cell lies above the detection threshold λ / σ 0 2 > d / n \lambda/\sigma_{0}^{2}>\sqrt{d/n} of the spiked-covariance model, with λ = μ 2 + τ 2 \lambda=\mu^{2}+\tau^{2} , so the collapse is caused by estimation error, not by a loss of detectability; we do not bound it. In one regime covariance reveals it; in another, isotropic covariance hides it until the first distinguishing moment, of order k ∗ k^{\ast} . Denoising-loss correlations are Stein discrepancies against a baseline and, for polynomial fields, exactly encode moment differences. Averaging noisy views of each clean point gives exact moment queries. In the covariance-matched regime, orientation-independent dictionaries satisfying an L 4 / L 2 L^{4}/L^{2} condition need order d k ∗ − 1 d^{k^{\ast}-1} features. The stated dot-product kernel ridge models need the same power in samples, as does small-step online SGD on one unit up to logarithms. A two-stage learner uses Gaussian-smoothed-loss curvature to recover the direction, then sharpens it and fits a scalar readout. For even k ∗ k^{\ast} , it obtains a fixed score gain over the Gaussian baseline from O ⁡ ( d k ∗ / 2 ​ log ⁡ d ) O(d^{k^{\ast}/2}\log d) clean points. In the covariance-visible regime, the frozen-feature threshold is d J / J ! d^{J}/J! ; projection onto principal components makes fitted-model, score-risk, and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension. Experiments are consistent with the spectral transition. A width-8 network trained with clean-point reuse shows a d 2 d^{2} -like training-set threshold over d = 64 d=64 – 192 192 , with fixed validation and calibration overhead. † † shortheadings: Denoising Is Stein / Rui Wang † † firstpage: 1 keywords diffusion models, denoising score matching, Stein discrepancies, feature learning, sample complexity 1 Introduction Diffusion models estimate the score ∇ log ⁡ p t 
abla\log p_{t} as Gaussian noise progressively obscures a data distribution ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . Training provides denoising pairs ( X 0 , X t ) (X_{0},X_{t}) : a clean point and a noisy view. The learner predicts X 0 X_{0} from X t X_{t} , thereby estimating the score ( Vincent, 2011 ) . If the data have a hidden non-Gaussian direction, a successful denoiser must detect it through those pairs. The amount of data needed depends on what the learner can represent and whether it can use repeated views of the same clean point. Existing theory studies parts of this question under different data models and resource measures. Lower bounds for random features and kernels count features or samples for fixed representations ( Ghorbani et al., 2021 ; Mei et al., 2022 ) ; analyses of trained denoisers count fresh pairs for one architecture and optimizer ( Bardone et al., 2026 ) ; statistical-query and cryptographic lower bounds count queries or computation for arbitrary algorithms ( Diakonikolas et al., 2017 ; Song, 2024 ) . These results do not directly compare the cost of learning the same hidden signal across learner classes. We ask: Which moments of a hidden structure can a denoising learner access, and how do representation size, distinct clean samples, noisy views and the learner’s access to geometry determine the cost of improving on the Gaussian score? We study two versions of one hidden-component model. In the covariance-visible regime ( σ 0 = 0 \sigma_{0}=0 ), the data lie on the subspace, their covariance reveals U U , and principal components recover it from k + 1 k+1 points. In the covariance-matched regime, Cov ⁡ ( Z ) = σ 0 2 ​ I k \mathrm{Cov}(Z)=\sigma_{0}^{2}I_{k} , so Cov ⁡ ( X 0 ) = σ 0 2 ​ I d \mathrm{Cov}(X_{0})=\sigma_{0}^{2}I_{d} carries no information about U U . The first informative moment has order k ∗ ≥ 3 k^{\ast}\geq 3 , the generative exponent of the latent law. Markers are measured 50% training-set thresholds from Section 7.2 ; they exclude the fixed 65,536 65{,}536 validation and calibration points, and cover only d = 64 d=64 – 192 192 . Contributions. The Stein–Tweedie identity expresses each residual correlation as a discrepancy between the noisy law and a baseline (Theorem 3.1 ); on polynomial fields, these correlations recover exactly the corresponding moment differences (Theorem 3.2 ). Thus a fitted Gaussian baseline removes the moments it matches, shifting the first accessible signal in the covariance-visible mixture from degree two to degree four (Theorem 3.4 , Corollary 3.6 ). Conditioning on the clean point gives an exact clean-data moment query (Lemma 3.3 ). Averaging fresh noisy views of one point reduces the forward-process variance of the corresponding gradient estimate. Diffusion acts on the hidden coordinate through an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck noise operator; the static signal-to-noise ratio of the best low-degree correlation peaks at the time in Theorem 3.8 . For an orientation-independent dictionary, the covariance-visible mixture has a sharp feature threshold at d 3 / 6 d^{3}/6 , with higher odd-degree steps at d J / J ! d^{J}/J! (Theorems 4.5 , 4.9 ). For one hidden direction, a one-sided change of measure identifies the height of the first step (Theorem 4.13 ). The covariance-matched model gives the d k ∗ − 1 d^{k^{\ast}-1} exponent for dictionaries satisfying the stated L 4 / L 2 L^{4}/L^{2} condition (Theorem 4.21 ). Kernel ridge regression on noisy inputs has the same sample exponent under the conditions of Theorem 5.2 ; for the exponential kernel this includes every ridge (Lemma 5.3 ). When covariance reveals the subspace, principal-component projection instead yields fitted-model, score-risk and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension (Theorems 4.15 , 4.16 ). Learning the covariance-matched direction can be cheaper than fixing a representation in advance. Small-step online SGD on one unit needs d k ∗ − 1 d^{k^{\ast}-1} steps up to log 2 ⁡ d \log^{2}d (Corollary 6.2 ), while the statistical-query bound gives tolerance d − k ∗ / 4 + o ( 1 ) d^{-k^{\ast}/4+o(1)} under its output-norm assumption (Proposition 6.3 ). Averaging r r noisy views of each clean point, one gradient step of the matrix score model recovers the direction from O ⁡ ( ( 1 + ( ι t − 1 ) / r ) ​ d k ∗ / 2 ​ log ⁡ d ) O((1+(\iota_{t}-1)/r)d^{k^{\ast}/2}\log d) clean points for even k ∗ k^{\ast} (Theorem 6.5 ). The same partial-trace matrix is the curvature created by Gaussian smoothing of a single-unit loss (Proposition 6.7 ). A learner that uses this curvature, sharpens the direction and fits a scalar readout obtains a fixed score gain with O ⁡ ( d k ∗ / 2 ​ log ⁡ d ) + O ⁡ ( d ) + O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(d^{k^{\ast}/2}\log d)+O(d)+O(1) clean points (Theorem 6.8 ). For k ∗ = 4 k^{\ast}=4 , this separates it from the restricted learner classes above by one power of d d , up to logarithms and under their stated hypotheses (Corollary 6.9 ). The experiments check the predicted barriers and invariances in the covariance-visible regime. In the covariance-matched regime, the partial trace’s measured overlaps are consistent with the proposed spectral transition within Monte Carlo error. A width-8 network trained with clean-point reuse has a d 2 d^{2} -like training-set threshold over d = 64 d=64 – 192 192 , with fixed validation and calibration overhead (Section 7 ). 1.2 Related work Low-dimensional structure in diffusion models. Chen et al. (2023a) give score approximation and estimation rates for data on a linear subspace, Oko et al. (2023) prove minimax optimality of diffusion estimators over Besov classes, and Li and Yan (2024) show that samplers adapt to unknown intrinsic dimension. Given an accurate score, sampling error is controlled by Chen et al. (2023b) and Benton et al. (2024) . These are upper bounds for adaptive estimators; our lower bounds identify what restricted classes lack, and our upper bounds count each resource separately. Fixed representations and kernels. Random-feature and kernel models in high dimension fit only polynomial components of degree ℓ \ell with d ℓ ≪ N d^{\ell}\ll N features or samples ( Ghorbani et al., 2019 ; Ghorbani et al., 2021 ; Mei et al., 2022 ) , and the spectrum of inner-product kernel matrices in polynomial regimes is described by Misiakiewicz (2022) and Lu and Yau (2022) . For denoising score matching, George et al. (2026) derive precise learning curves for random features and George and Macris (2026) extend them to manifold data. Here the inputs are non-Gaussian along a hidden direction, and the barrier applies to every orientation-blind dictionary with arbitrary coefficients. For one hidden direction, it also gives the exact risk height relative to the moment-matched Gaussian denoiser. Exponents, statistical queries and non-Gaussian component analysis. The information exponent governs online SGD for single-index models ( Ben Arous et al., 2021 ) , and the generative exponent governs statistical-query and low-degree algorithms ( Damian et al., 2024 ) . Statistical-query lower bounds for non-Gaussian component analysis are due to Diakonikolas et al. (2017) and Diakonikolas et al. (2024) , spectral algorithms to Vempala and Xiao (2011) and Tan and Vershynin (2018) , and score estimation for such data is cryptographically hard in general ( Song, 2024 ) . Bardone et al. (2026) show that a denoiser trained online on a mixed cumulant model learns pair-wise statistics at linear cost and the fourth cumulant at cubic cost, defining a diffusion information exponent; Székely et al. (2024) report a quadratic sample threshold for supervised networks in a spiked cumulant model. Our Theorem 3.2 identifies the generative exponent as the relevant one for denoising, and Corollary 3.6 gives a mechanism for the staged learning of Bardone et al. (2026) . Tensor methods, smoothing and reuse. The fourth-moment tensor of non-Gaussian component data is a spiked tensor, for which unfolding reaches d k / 2 d^{k/2} ( Montanari and Richard, 2014 ) and gradient descent or Langevin dynamics from random starts needs d k − 1 d^{k-1} ( Ben Arous et al., 2020 ) . Gaussian smoothing reaches the unfolding threshold for tensor PCA ( Anandkumar et al., 2017 ) and the d k / 2 d^{k/2} rate for online single-index learning ( Damian et al., 2023 ) ; SGD can be viewed as optimizing a smoothed objective ( Kleinberg et al., 2018 ) . Reusing batches changes what gradient methods can learn in supervised two-layer networks ( Dandi et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) . A link between one gradient step of a diffusion objective and a spectral method was made for a covariance spike by Shah et al. (2023) . Here the conditional Stein identity connects reuse to the denoising loss, and the curvature created by smoothing is the partial-trace statistic. The resulting two-stage learner has explicit costs for clean points, noisy views and arithmetic. Stein’s method and score matching. Theorem 3.1 is a standard consequence of Stein’s lemma and Tweedie’s formula ( Robbins, 1956 ; Efron, 2011 ) ; its supremum over a unit ball of fields is a Stein discrepancy ( Gorham and Mackey, 2015 ) , and the equivalence of denoising score matching with score matching is due to Hyvärinen (2005) and Vincent (2011) . We use this identity to compare what different denoising learners can extract from the same hidden-component model. 2 Setting, learners and resources 2.1 Diffusion pairs, denoisers and baselines Fix a time t > 0 t>0 and write a = a t = e − t a=a_{t}=e^{-t} , h = h t = 1 − e − 2 ​ t h=h_{t}=1-e^{-2t} . Corollary 3.6 (Gaussian preconditioning shifts the exponent) . Suppose P 0 P_{0} has an anisotropic covariance with range U U , as in Assumption 2 . Against an isotropic baseline the first moment mismatch is at order two, and correlations with linear fields reveal U U . Against the Gaussian fitted to the first two moments, correlations with fields of degree at most one vanish; if the latent law is centrally symmetric, those of degree two vanish as well; and if its fourth cumulant tensor is nonzero (for the two-component mixture it is − 2 ​ μ 4 -2\mu^{4} per coordinate), the first nonzero correlation has degree three and the exponent is four. Corollary 3.6 is the mechanism behind the two regimes. In the covariance-visible regime the Gaussian part of the score teaches the geometry: correlations of degree one reveal the subspace at linear cost. A learner that subtracts the fitted Gaussian, or a frozen representation that cannot use the covariance, faces exponent four, and Section 4 shows that it pays a cubic price. It also explains the staged learning observed by Bardone et al. (2026) : once a model has fitted the Gaussian part of the score, the correlations it can still exploit are of order at least three. 3.4 Diffusion time Theorem 3.7 (Exact action of the forward process) .
